288.title: Live by nature
288.hook: Zeno's goal: live in agreement with nature (Diogenes Laërtius 7.87)
288.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism today read 'living by nature' as living up to reason and fellowship, and some make a habit of time outdoors as a reminder of the larger order.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eupatheia, the good feelings the Stoics kept: joy, wise wishing, caution. Your line was joy is allowed.

Live by nature. Put those words on a label and they'll sell you almost anything. Granola. Face cream. A cabin in the woods with no wifi. Barefoot running shoes, a strange idea if you think about it. So when you hear that the founder of the Stoics said the whole point of life is to live in agreement with nature, you might picture a man in a toga hugging a tree. That's not what Zeno meant. What he meant is stranger, and more useful. We're still on the porch, now in the Stoic world.
screen: `LIVE BY NATURE, ON A LABEL.` → `NOT A TOGA HUGGING A TREE.` → `LIVE BY NATURE.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius reports that Zeno, in a book called On the Nature of Man, was the first to say the goal of life is to live in agreement with nature, and that this is the same as living by virtue. There's a small puzzle in the sources. Another ancient report says Zeno's own phrase was shorter: just live in agreement. Live consistently, all of a piece, not at war with yourself. His successors, it says, added the words with nature. Scholars still discuss which is right. Either way, the idea grew to hold two natures. The first is your own. For the Stoics, a human is an animal that reasons and lives with others. A fish lives by its nature when it swims; a human lives by hers when she thinks clearly and treats people well. Living by nature means living up to the human part of you. The second is the nature of the whole world. Chrysippus said our nature is part of the nature of everything, and the good life fits the pattern of the whole, like a note that fits a song. So, not a cabin in the woods: a Stoic could live by nature in a city office. Still, Marcus Aurelius looked closely at ordinary natural things. In one passage of his notebook he notices figs splitting open, ripe olives, the cracks on a baked loaf, a lion's brow, and says they have their own beauty because they belong to the order of things. Agreement with yourself, with others, with the whole.
screen: `ZENO: LIVE IN AGREEMENT WITH NATURE.` · `ALL OF A PIECE, NOT AT WAR.` · `YOUR NATURE: REASON AND OTHERS.` · `THE NATURE OF THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `IN AGREEMENT.`

segments.voice: If you can, face a window or step outside; if not, picture the last tree you saw. Look at one living thing, a plant, a bird, a patch of sky, simply doing what it is. Then notice your own breath doing what it does, your mind noticing: for now, you and the tree are in agreement.
Zeno. The Stoic founder who said the goal of life is to live in agreement with your own nature and the nature of the whole.
Your line: in agreement. All of a piece, inside and out, wherever you are. See you tomorrow.

289.title: The reason in things
289.hook: Stoics saw a reason running through all things
289.howItsDone: Many who practice Stoicism today treat the logos as the rational order of nature, whether they understand it religiously or not, and try to think clearly as their share in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zeno, and his goal, to live in agreement with nature. Your line was in agreement.

Cut an apple across the middle, not top to bottom, and you'll find a five-pointed star. A sunflower's seeds curl out in two sets of spirals, one clockwise, one counter. Your heartbeat speeds up on the stairs and settles when you sit. The tide comes in about twice a day, a little later each day. None of it looks random. There's an order to things, and the Stoics gave that order a name: logos.
screen: `A STAR INSIDE AN APPLE.` → `SPIRALS IN A SUNFLOWER.` → `THERE'S AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Logos is a very busy Greek word: word, speech, story, account, reason, even ratio. It comes from a verb meaning to say, and before that, to gather or pick out. You hear it in logic, or biology, the account of life. Long before Zeno, a philosopher named Heraclitus of Ephesus used logos for the order behind the world, and complained that it's common to all of us, yet most people live as if they had a private understanding of their own. The Stoics built on it. For them, the logos is the reason running through everything, the rational pattern that shapes a seed into a tree and keeps the stars in their tracks. They pictured it as active and alive, a kind of fiery breath moving through matter, and gave it many names at once: nature, fate, providence, even Zeus or God. Stoics disagreed among themselves about details, and the sources are fragmentary, so it's fair to say we only see the outline. Here's why it matters for a person, not just the cosmos. Each of us, they said, carries a small share of that same reason. When you think clearly, you're doing on a small scale what the world does on a large one. That's why living by reason and living by nature were the same thing to them. The same Greek word appears in the Gospel of John, where Christians read it their own way; for the Stoics, the logos was the pattern itself.
screen: `LOGOS — WORD, REASON, ACCOUNT.` · `HERACLITUS: COMMON TO ALL.` · `A REASON RUNNING THROUGH EVERYTHING.` · `A SMALL SHARE IN EACH OF US.` · then, large: `THE PATTERN.`

segments.voice: Start with the nearest pattern: your breath. In, a turn at the top, out, a pause at the bottom; nobody is running it, and it runs. If your mind wanders, that's a pattern too: come back, one turn, then the next.
Logos. Greek for word, reason or account: for the Stoics, the reason running through all things, shared in each of us.
Your line: the pattern. A seed, a star, a clear thought: one reason running through them all. That's day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: All woven together
290.hook: think of the universe as one living being, all things woven (Meditations 4.40)
290.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners use Marcus Aurelius's exercise of picturing the universe as one living whole, and reflect on the many people whose work sustains their day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: logos, the reason running through all things. Your line was the pattern.

Pick up the nearest cup. Somebody dug the clay or melted the sand. Somebody fired it in a kiln; somebody else built the kiln. A truck driver carried it on a road a crew paved, in a truck built in a factory somewhere you've never been. Now the coffee inside: a farmer on a hillside, a picker, a roaster, a ship's crew. You're holding more people's work than you could count, in one hand, and you'll never meet most of them. The Stoics had a word for that feeling of everything touching everything. Today: sympatheia.
screen: `PICK UP THE NEAREST CUP.` → `MORE HANDS THAN YOU CAN COUNT.` → `SYMPATHEIA.`

segments.voice: Sympatheia is Greek: sym, together, plus pathos, feeling or being affected. Being affected together. It's the root of our word sympathy, but the Stoics meant something bigger than feeling sorry for someone: every part of the world is connected to every other, so what happens in one place is felt in another. One example they reached for was the moon and the sea. The Stoic Posidonius, a scientist as well as a philosopher, studied how the tides rise and fall with the moon, and saw in it a sign of one connected cosmos. Marcus Aurelius made it a daily exercise. In George Long's 1862 translation, he tells himself: "Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul." He pictures all things working together as causes of one another, like threads spun into a single web. Elsewhere he writes that all things are bound up with each other, and in that way friendly to each other. Why did this matter to an emperor? On this view, if everything is woven together, no one is truly a stranger, and no act is truly private. How you treat the person who made your cup, even without meeting them, is part of the same fabric. A warning, honestly given: the Stoics also used sympatheia to defend astrology and divination, and ancient critics, Cicero among them, pushed back hard. The idea comes as a package, and readers sort it differently. The plainest part of it is the cup in your hand: it carries the work of people you'll never meet.
screen: `SYM + PATHEIA: AFFECTED TOGETHER.` · `THE MOON AND THE SEA.` · `ONE LIVING BEING, ONE WEB.` · `NO ONE IS TRULY A STRANGER.` · then, large: `ALL WOVEN.`

segments.voice: Choose one object near you, your shirt, a chair, the phone in your hand, and trace it backward one pair of hands at a time: who sewed it, grew it, mined it, packed it, drove it? You won't know their names; picture them anyway. With each breath, add one more person to the web.
Sympatheia. Greek for being affected together: the Stoic idea that all things are connected, one woven whole.
Your line: all woven. One living being, one web, with you somewhere in it. More tomorrow.

291.title: Hierocles' circles
291.hook: picture circles of care, self, family, town, humanity, and draw them inward (Hierocles, in Stobaeus)
291.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners sometimes picture Hierocles' concentric circles and deliberately treat people in outer circles with the care usually kept for inner ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sympatheia, everything in the world affected together. Your line was all woven.

Watch a baby for an afternoon. First she cares about herself: warm, fed, held. Soon she knows her mother's face from every other face. Then her dad, a sibling, the dog. Later, a best friend; later still, a whole school she'll cheer for at a game. Care grows outward in rings, like a stone dropped in a pond. The Stoics noticed this too, and thought it wasn't only a story about growing up. It was an assignment for adults.
screen: `A BABY CARES FOR HERSELF.` → `THEN A FACE, A FAMILY, A FRIEND.` → `RINGS IN A POND.`

segments.voice: Oikeiosis is a hard word to translate. It comes from oikos, house or home, and means something like making your own, or coming to feel at home with. The Stoics said every living creature starts with oikeiosis toward itself: it cares for its own life. In humans that care keeps widening, until we feel at home with more and more of the world. Hierocles, a later Stoic, turned this into a picture, and we know it because a later collector named Stobaeus copied it into his anthology. Imagine yourself surrounded by circles. The smallest holds your own mind and body. The next, your parents, siblings, partner, children. Then aunts, uncles, cousins. Then your neighbors, your town, your country. The biggest holds the whole human race. Here's the practical part, and it's charming. The job, Hierocles says, is to draw the circles inward, pulling each ring a little closer to the center. His tip: speak of cousins as brothers and sisters, of uncles and aunts as fathers and mothers. Words change how near people feel. You don't pretend a stranger is your child; you just move them in one ring. Most of what Hierocles wrote was lost, until a papyrus with part of his ethics turned up in Egypt. So this picture survived by two thin threads, an anthology and a scrap of papyrus, and now it's in your ear. Draw the circles in.
screen: `OIKEIOSIS — MAKING YOUR OWN.` · `CIRCLES FROM SELF TO HUMANITY.` · `PULL EACH RING CLOSER.` · `CALL COUSINS BROTHERS AND SISTERS.` · then, large: `DRAW THE CIRCLES IN.`

segments.voice: Picture the circles around you: you at the center, your closest people, your wider family, your street or your coworkers, your town, your country, everyone. Find one person out in an outer ring, a neighbor you nod to, a coworker you barely know. On each breath in, bring them one ring closer, just one, and notice how it feels to hold them there.
Oikeiosis. Greek for making your own, feeling at home with: care that starts with the self and widens to all people.
Your line: draw the circles in. A cousin called a sister is already one ring nearer. Two hundred ninety-one days now.

292.title: Citizen of the world
292.hook: asked where he came from, Diogenes said he was a citizen of the world (Diogenes Laërtius 6.63)
292.carry: a bigger home around the smaller one
292.howItsDone: People drawn to Stoic cosmopolitanism keep their local loyalties while trying to treat people everywhere as fellow citizens of one human community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: oikeiosis, Hierocles' circles of care. Your line was draw the circles in.

Where are you from? It's the first question at a party, on a form, at a border, and the answer sorts people into ours and theirs in about two seconds. Now picture a scruffy old man in the market in Athens, the one who told Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight. Somebody asks him where he's from. He could say Sinope, the town on the Black Sea where he was born, and which threw him out. Instead he gives an answer nobody had given before. Today: kosmopolitēs.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU FROM?` → `OURS AND THEIRS IN TWO SECONDS.` → `KOSMOPOLITĒS.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius reports that when Diogenes the Cynic was asked where he came from, he said: I am a citizen of the world. In Greek, kosmopolitēs: kosmos, the ordered universe, plus politēs, citizen of a polis, a city. It's the first time we find the word, and it's the root of our cosmopolitan. Remember, Diogenes wasn't a Stoic. He was a Cynic, like Crates, the man Zeno followed out of a bookshop back on day twenty-six. But the Stoics took the idea and made it central. In a Greek world where your city was your identity, your law, your gods and your army, saying my city is the world was almost shocking. Epictetus told his students not to answer I'm an Athenian or I'm a Corinthian, but to think of themselves as citizens of the whole. Seneca said each of us belongs to two communities: the small one we happen to be born into, and the great one that holds gods and humans together. And Marcus Aurelius, who was actually running an empire, wrote something like this: as Antoninus, my city is Rome; as a human being, it's the world. He didn't give up Rome. He kept both. That's the Stoic version: not no home, but a bigger home around the smaller one. It's yesterday's outermost circle, taken seriously, as if the people there were your neighbors too.
screen: `KOSMOS + POLITĒS: WORLD CITIZEN.` · `A CYNIC SAID IT FIRST.` · `TWO COMMUNITIES, SMALL AND GREAT.` · `ROME AS ANTONINUS, THE WORLD AS HUMAN.` · then, large: `CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you'd name if someone asked where you're from: its streets, its weather, its food, and let that be home. Then let the picture widen, the country around it, the ocean past that, a city on the other side of the world where someone is waking up as you breathe. Hold both, the small home and the big one, and breathe.
Kosmopolitēs. Greek for citizen of the world: Diogenes' answer to where are you from, taken up by the Stoics.
Your line: a bigger home around the smaller one. Rome as Antoninus, the world as a human being. Until tomorrow.

293.title: Want what happens
293.hook: Epictetus: wish things to happen as they do, and life will go well (Enchiridion 8)
293.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners try to meet events outside their control with acceptance, even welcome, while still acting on what is up to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world. Your line was a bigger home around the smaller one.
screen: `KOSMOPOLITĒS — A BIGGER HOME AROUND THE SMALLER ONE.`

segments.voice: It's raining on the day of the picnic. The flight is delayed three hours. The recipe you've made twenty times comes out flat. The usual move is to argue with it. This shouldn't be happening. It was supposed to be sunny. It's not fair. And the arguing goes on for an hour after the rain has soaked the sandwiches. The Stoics thought the arguing hurts more than the rain, and proposed something that sounds almost impossible. Don't just put up with what happens. Want it.
screen: `RAIN ON THE PICNIC.` → `THIS SHOULDN'T BE HAPPENING.` → `WANT IT.`

segments.voice: Start with a surprise about the word. Amor fati is Latin for love of fate, and it sounds like an ancient Stoic motto. It isn't. No Stoic on record used the phrase. It comes from the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, in the 1880s, who wanted to love everything that happens, not just bear it. But the idea is much older, and Epictetus put it plainly in his Handbook. In George Long's translation: "Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life." Flip the direction of the wish. The early Stoics had a picture for it, reported by a later writer. A dog is tied to a moving cart. If it wants to go where the cart goes, it trots along, freely. If not, it gets dragged anyway. Same road, different trip. Seneca, putting verses by the Stoic Cleanthes into Latin, ends them with one line: the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling. Now the honest part, so this doesn't turn into giving up. Remember the dichotomy of control from the weeks of practices: some things are up to us, some aren't. Amor fati is for the second column. If the rain is falling, want the rain. But if you can fix the leak, fix the leak. Wanting what happens isn't pretending you don't care. It's refusing to spend your life arguing with what already is, so your strength goes to what's still yours to do.
screen: `AMOR FATI — NIETZSCHE'S PHRASE.` · `WISH THINGS TO BE AS THEY ARE.` · `THE DOG AND THE CART.` · `ONLY FOR WHAT ISN'T UP TO US.` · then, large: `LOVE WHAT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing today that didn't go your way and can't be changed now, and check whether some part of you is still arguing with it. Try the flip, silently, as an experiment: all right, this is how it went; then, if you can manage it, i'll take it. Breathe with that, and see what loosens.
Amor fati. Latin for love of fate: Nietzsche's phrase for an old Stoic idea, wanting what happens instead of arguing with it.
Your line: love what happens. The willing dog and the dragged one travel the same road. Day two hundred ninety-three, and counting.

294.title: The citadel
294.hook: a mind free from passions is a citadel, Marcus writes (Meditations 8.48)
294.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners take short pauses during the day to retreat inward, as Marcus Aurelius describes, instead of waiting for a vacation to find calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amor fati, love of fate. Your line was love what happens.

Many old Greek cities had one: a fortress on the highest ground. When raiders came up the valley, the farmers and families ran uphill, through the gates, and the walls held. In Athens it's the Acropolis, where the Parthenon still stands. Now picture an emperor in an army camp on the northern frontier, with a long war on his hands. He has no hill to run to. So he writes himself a note about the one fortress nobody can take. Today: the citadel.
screen: `A FORTRESS ON THE HIGH GROUND.` → `AN EMPEROR WITH NO HILL.` → `THE CITADEL.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius wrote his notebook in Greek, and in book eight he uses the word for a city's fortress, akropolis. In George Long's translation, he writes that "the mind which is free from passions is a citadel". Nothing, he goes on, is more secure for a person to flee to. Remember passions from last week: not all feeling, but the runaway kind, built on a mistaken judgment. So the citadel isn't a numb mind. It's a mind that hasn't said yes to the panic. Earlier in the Meditations he makes the point another way. People look for retreats, houses in the country, the seashore, the mountains. But you can retreat into yourself any time you like, and there's no quieter place. It doesn't take a vacation. It takes a minute. The historian Pierre Hadot named a whole book about Marcus after this image, The Inner Citadel. And it gathers up this week. Zeno, in agreement. The logos, the pattern. Sympatheia, all woven. Hierocles' circles, drawn in. A bigger home around the smaller one. Amor fati, love what happens. Each one widened the view to the whole cosmos; the citadel brings it back to one quiet room inside you. That's the Stoic shape: the biggest possible world, and a small, steady center from which to meet it. One honest note. Marcus wrote this for himself, not for us, and some readers hear a man reminding himself because he kept forgetting. If so, the citadel wasn't a place he lived. It was a place he kept walking back to.
screen: `AKROPOLIS: THE HIGH FORTRESS.` · `A MIND FREE FROM PASSIONS.` · `RETREAT INTO YOURSELF.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD, A STEADY CENTER.` · then, large: `THE CITADEL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and picture a path going uphill; walk it to a gate at the top, step through, and let it close behind you. The noise of the day is outside the walls now: you can still hear it, it just can't come in. Rest inside, breathing.
The citadel. Marcus Aurelius's image for a mind free from runaway passions: a fortress you can retreat into anytime.
Your line: one quiet room inside you. That's the week in the Stoic world; next week, the Stoics honestly. Rest well.
